disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced. Self‑worth is often tightly linked to weight control, with individuals frequently denying the seriousness of their low weight. Onset is most common in adolescence and young adulthood but can occur or recur later in life, sometimes triggered by major stressors, medical events, or role transitions. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the prominence of restriction (rather than binge‑purge cycles as in bulimia nervosa) and by the centrality of weight phobia and body‑image distortion in the clinical picture.

narrative.personality: She is a meticulous, routine‑driven retiree who takes quiet pride in being the most dependable and organized member of her church and senior community.
narrative.stressor: Two years ago, Zilma’s primary care doctor warned her that her blood pressure and blood sugar were creeping up and advised her to "watch her weight" and "trim down" to stay healthy enough to keep up her activities. Already someone who equated being dependable with being disciplined and in control, she latched onto the idea that maintaining a smaller body was the key to remaining useful in her roles as gardener, cook, and church meals liaison. Over time, she began to scrutinize her appearance and compare herself with other thin, active women in her senior group, gradually tightening her eating rules under the guise of "healthy living" and taking pride in every pound she lost as proof of her self‑control. Her family and choir friends eventually became worried about how frail she looked and how preoccupied she seemed with looking "trim and tidy," and after she dismissed their concerns, her pastor and daughter together convinced her to see a psychiatrist when she started avoiding social meals at church and became upset by small fluctuations in her weight.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t stand the idea of getting bigger again; I feel like I have to keep my body small and neat or I’ve let myself go.”

narrative.personality: She is an outgoing, hard‑working woman who thrives on routine and community connection, even as she wrestles with occasional disorganization and a tendency to be hard on herself.
narrative.stressor: After her divorce three years ago, Judy threw herself into work and church activities, but comments from her ex‑husband about her weight and appearance lingered, feeding a sense that she had been "too much" in every way. As she began dating again, well‑meaning remarks from friends about "getting her figure back" and social media images of very slim women left her increasingly self‑conscious, particularly given her love of Southern cooking and family gatherings centered around rich meals. Wanting to prove to herself and others that she had control over her life after the breakup, she started making stricter and stricter rules around food and celebrating every sign that she was getting smaller, while quietly dreading anything that might cause the scale to go up. When coworkers and church friends began to express alarm at how gaunt she looked and how anxious she became about eating at potlucks or family fish fries, her adult daughter insisted she see a psychiatrist, especially after Judy admitted she was terrified that "if I gain any weight back, nobody will want me."
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m scared that if I gain any weight back I’ll lose control and get fat again, and that thought just terrifies me.”

narrative.personality: He is a sociable, curious retiree who channels his talkative energy and underlying anxiety into meticulous planning of community art and social activities.
narrative.stressor: When Michael formally retired from his long‑standing volunteer leadership role and shifted into a less structured senior‑outreach position, he struggled with the loss of a clear identity and daily schedule. Around the same time, several of his peers developed serious health problems that he associated with "letting themselves go," triggering anxiety about aging, dependence, and losing relevance in the intergenerational art programs he loved. Looking for something concrete he could control, he began to treat his eating and weight like another project to manage, meticulously tracking portions and cutting back more and more while telling himself he was just "staying lean and sharp" to keep up with younger volunteers and participants. Over months, friends at the senior center noticed how thin and tired he looked and how often he declined shared meals after workshops, and when he finally admitted to a fellow organizer that he felt he "couldn’t relax" his strict eating rules without everything in his life slipping, they encouraged him to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve gotten so strict with what I allow myself to eat that it’s starting to run my life, but I feel like I can’t loosen up without losing control.”
